content: When a hypothesis test calls an outcome extreme, how is that determined from the test statistic? I am especially unsure how the definition changes between one-sided and two-sided tests.

"Extreme" is defined by the alternative hypothesis and the test statistic before interpreting the data. For a one-sided test, it usually means values at least as far into the specified tail as the observed statistic. For a two-sided test, it means outcomes comparably inconsistent with the null in either direction. The exact two-sided calculation can depend on the statistic and test, so it is not always simply twice one tail.
Could you illustrate that with a coin-flipping example where the null says the coin is fair? Please compare observing too many heads with observing an unusual imbalance in either direction.

Suppose 100 flips produce 62 heads. A one-sided test for a heads-favoring coin counts, under a fair coin, the probability of 62 or more heads. A two-sided test for any departure from fairness also counts comparably unlikely outcomes on the low side, commonly 38 or fewer heads in this symmetric setting. Thus the reference set of outcomes, and consequently the p-value, depends on the prespecified alternative.

I might be wrong, but I think a p-value is the probability, assuming the null model, of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed? That seems to match the tail calculation you described.

Yes, that is the standard interpretation, with "extreme" defined by the chosen test statistic and alternative. The assumption matters: the probability is calculated within the null model, including any sampling and independence assumptions. It refers to the observed result plus more extreme possibilities, not merely the probability of the exact observation. It also does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis itself.
If the coin produced exactly 62 heads twice in separate sets of 100 flips, would each experiment have the same p-value, or could design choices make them differ?

They match only if the null model, stopping rule, test statistic, sidedness, and analysis plan match. If one experiment stopped after exactly 100 flips while another stopped according to a data-dependent rule, their reference distributions may differ. Likewise, a prespecified one-sided test and a two-sided test produce different p-values. The numerical outcome alone does not fully determine the inferential calculation.
Why do people distinguish the probability of data given a hypothesis from the probability of a hypothesis given data? The phrases sound similar, but apparently they lead to different conclusions.

They reverse the conditioning. A hypothesis test can calculate how surprising certain data would be if a null hypothesis and its assumptions held. That is a statement about data under a model. A probability for the hypothesis after seeing data is a posterior probability, which requires a framework such as Bayes' theorem, a prior probability for competing hypotheses, and likelihoods for the observed evidence. One conditional probability does not determine the other.
Suppose a medical trial reports a p-value of 0.03 for no treatment difference. What can be said directly from that number, before considering prior evidence or study quality?

Under the specified null model, the chosen test would produce a result at least as extreme as the observed one about 3% of the time in repeated sampling. That interpretation presumes the test was selected appropriately and its assumptions hold. The number alone does not reveal the probability that the treatment works, the probability the null is true, the effect's magnitude, or whether bias affected the trial.

I might be wrong, but I think a p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true after obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed? Is that the relevant conditional probability?

The conditioning runs the other way. A p-value describes the probability of results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null model; it is not the probability that the null is true after the results. To estimate the latter, a Bayesian analysis would combine prior probabilities with the likelihood of the actual data under the null and alternatives. Different priors and alternative models can therefore yield different posterior probabilities even with the same p-value.
Could two studies with identical p-values therefore support different posterior probabilities for their null hypotheses if one tests an established mechanism and the other tests an implausible one?

Yes. Identical p-values need not imply identical posterior probabilities. Prior plausibility can differ, and the alternative hypotheses may predict the observed data with different strength. Study design and measurement reliability also affect the appropriate likelihoods. A Bayesian comparison makes those ingredients explicit; a p-value does not encode them. This is why the surrounding scientific evidence remains important even when the reported test statistics coincide.
How can a study find a very small p-value for a difference that looks numerically tiny? I would like to understand the role played by sample size and measurement variability.

A test statistic commonly scales the estimated effect by its standard error. With a very large sample or low variability, the standard error can become small, so even a tiny estimated difference lies many standard errors from the null value and produces a small p-value. Conversely, a substantial effect measured imprecisely may not do so. Statistical detectability therefore depends on effect magnitude, sample size, variability, and the test's assumptions.
Would reporting a confidence interval alongside the p-value address this? For example, could it show that the plausible effect sizes are all too small to matter in practice?

It helps considerably. A confidence interval displays an estimate together with its sampling uncertainty, in the effect's original units when possible. You can compare the interval with a prespecified threshold for practical importance. An interval may exclude the null value while remaining entirely within a practically trivial range. Interpretation should also consider design quality, multiplicity, and whether that importance threshold was chosen for substantive reasons.
I might be wrong, but I think a small p-value measures incompatibility with the null model, not the size or practical importance of the observed effect? That would explain the tiny difference.

That is a useful distinction. A small p-value says the data are relatively incompatible with the specified null model, as summarized by the chosen statistic. It does not put the effect into meaningful units or decide whether anyone should care about its magnitude. For that, examine the effect estimate, confidence interval, and domain-specific importance threshold. Also check whether model assumptions or a large sample made a small discrepancy especially detectable.
If a confidence interval excludes zero but also excludes every effect considered worthwhile, what would be a clear way to summarize both the statistical and practical conclusions?

You might say: "The estimated effect was statistically distinguishable from zero under the model, but the confidence interval lay entirely below the prespecified threshold for practical importance." Then report the estimate, interval, threshold, and its rationale. Avoid calling the result simply "significant," because that can blur two separate judgments. If the threshold was selected after seeing the data, disclose that exploratory choice.
When comparing two published studies, is the one with the smaller p-value necessarily showing the stronger or more consequential effect? What information would make that comparison meaningful?

No. A smaller p-value can reflect a larger effect, but also a larger sample, lower noise, a different test, or different modeling assumptions. Compare effect estimates in commensurate units, their uncertainty intervals, study designs, and thresholds of practical relevance. If outcomes use different scales, a standardized effect may help, though its substantive meaning still needs care. Directly ranking scientific importance by p-values alone is usually misleading.
Imagine one intervention lowers blood pressure by a fraction of a unit in a huge sample, while another lowers it several units in a small sample. How should their results be described?

Report each estimated change and confidence interval first, then its p-value if relevant. The huge study may estimate a very small change precisely and yield a small p-value. The small study may estimate a larger change but leave substantial uncertainty. Clinical importance should be judged against a defensible blood-pressure threshold and possible harms, not against which p-value is lower. Differences in populations and design may also limit direct comparison.
I might be wrong, but I think a small p-value measures the size and practical importance of the observed effect, not merely incompatibility with the null model? Would that favor the huge study?

A small p-value does not by itself measure effect size or practical importance. It summarizes how incompatible the result is with the null model through a statistic whose value also depends on precision. The huge study could therefore have the smaller p-value for a clinically negligible change. To compare consequences, use the estimated changes, uncertainty intervals, relevant clinical thresholds, harms, and costs. Those quantities might favor either intervention, regardless of the p-value ranking.
Are standardized effect sizes enough to settle the comparison, or can an apparently large standardized effect still have limited practical value because of the outcome and setting?

Standardization helps compare effects measured on different scales, but it does not settle practical value. A standardized effect depends on the population's variability, which may differ across settings, and it can hide the original units. Practical value also depends on the outcome's importance, baseline risk, duration, side effects, feasibility, and cost. Whenever possible, present standardized and raw-unit effects together, with uncertainty and a substantively justified benchmark.
What exactly changes when a test result crosses a conventional threshold such as 0.05? Does that boundary alter the underlying evidence, or only the decision made under a rule?

Crossing the threshold changes the binary decision under that testing rule: reject or fail to reject the null. It does not create a sharp scientific difference between, say, p = 0.049 and p = 0.051. The p-value varies continuously, while the cutoff is a chosen error-control convention. Interpretation should retain the estimate, uncertainty, design, and consequences of errors rather than treating the boundary as a discovery switch.

Suppose an observational study rejects a null association between air pollution and hospital visits. Which additional questions are needed before interpreting the association as consequential or explanatory?

Ask how large the association is, how precisely it is estimated, and whether that magnitude matters for health or policy. Then assess confounding, selection, measurement error, time trends, model choices, and multiple analyses. Temporality, dose-response patterns, negative controls, natural experiments, and consistency with other evidence may strengthen a causal account. Rejecting a null association is one piece of evidence, not a substitute for those design and causal considerations.

I might be wrong, but I think rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold does not establish that the alternative explanation is practically important or causal? It only triggers the test decision.

That framing is sound. Rejection says the observed data meet a rule for incompatibility with the null model, conditional on the test and its assumptions. Practical importance requires an effect magnitude, uncertainty, and a meaningful benchmark. Causality requires an identification argument grounded in design and assumptions. Moreover, rejecting one null does not automatically validate a single alternative explanation; several causal and noncausal mechanisms may fit the same association.
Would lowering the threshold to 0.005 solve either issue, or would it mainly demand stronger evidence against the null while leaving practical importance and causality separate?

It mainly makes rejection harder and, under specified conditions, reduces the long-run rate of certain false rejections. It does not turn the p-value into an effect-size measure or repair confounding and other causal threats. A stricter cutoff can be useful in some high-multiplicity or high-stakes settings, but practical importance still needs substantive benchmarks, and causality still depends on design, identification assumptions, and corroborating evidence.
How should causal language be handled when a regression coefficient is statistically significant? I often see the predictor described as a cause even when the data are observational.

Statistical significance alone supports neither the causal label nor a particular mechanism. In observational data, the coefficient may reflect confounding, selection, reverse causation, measurement choices, or model misspecification. Causal wording needs a credible identification strategy, such as random assignment or well-defended quasi-experimental assumptions, plus appropriate analysis. Without that basis, describe the result as an adjusted association and state which variables and assumptions the adjustment involved.
Consider a regression where neighborhood park access predicts lower stress scores with p below 0.05. What would prevent the coefficient from demonstrating a meaningful causal benefit of parks?

Neighborhood income, residential self-selection, safety, traffic, healthcare access, and measurement differences could influence both park access and stress. The estimated score difference might also be too small to matter, even if precisely measured. A causal claim would require a design or assumptions that address such competing paths, while practical importance requires interpreting the effect in score units or a more tangible outcome. The threshold alone handles neither question.
I might be wrong, but I think rejecting a null hypothesis at a chosen threshold establishes that the alternative explanation is practically important and causal? Is that what the decision licenses?

The decision is narrower than that. Rejection indicates that the data are sufficiently incompatible with the tested null under a chosen rule and model assumptions. It does not determine whether the estimated difference is large enough to matter, and it does not eliminate confounding or identify a causal pathway. For the park example, inspect the effect estimate and uncertainty for importance, then evaluate the study's identification strategy before using causal language.
If the study used a policy change that assigned new parks to some neighborhoods, which features of that change would make the causal interpretation more credible?

Credibility would improve if park assignment were unrelated to neighborhoods' potential stress trends, implementation timing were plausibly exogenous, and comparison neighborhoods showed parallel pre-policy trends. Check for simultaneous policies, migration, spillovers, selective compliance, and changes in measurement. An interrupted rollout or lottery could offer stronger leverage. Report balance and falsification checks, but remember that each design rests on assumptions that should be defended rather than inferred from significance.
What should be concluded when a hypothesis test returns p = 0.28? I am trying to separate absence of evidence from evidence that an effect is absent.

At conventional thresholds, p = 0.28 means the test does not reject the null. By itself, that result may arise because the null is a good approximation, because the study is imprecise, or because the test has low sensitivity to the relevant effect. Examine the effect estimate, confidence interval, sample size, measurement quality, and power for substantively important alternatives before deciding how much evidence there is for absence.
How does the width of a confidence interval help distinguish those possibilities? Could a wide interval make the same non-rejection compatible with both meaningful benefit and meaningful harm?

Exactly. A wide interval signals limited precision and may include the null alongside effects large enough to be beneficial or harmful. Such a result is inconclusive about those possibilities. A narrow interval centered near the null can be more informative, especially if it excludes effects beyond prespecified importance bounds. The interval does not prove every included value equally plausible, but it makes the range of estimates compatible with the procedure visible.
I might be wrong, but I think failing to reject the null means the data lack sufficient evidence against it, not that the null has been proven true? The interval seems important here.

Yes. Failure to reject is a statement about insufficient evidence against the null under the chosen test, not a proof that the null is true. The confidence interval helps reveal whether the data are merely imprecise or whether they constrain the effect near the null. If the scientific aim is to show effects are negligibly small, use an equivalence test or interval-based criterion with meaningful bounds designed for that question.
Could you explain how an equivalence test reverses the usual setup, and why choosing the equivalence bounds before looking at the results matters for interpretation?

In an equivalence test, the null typically includes effects at or beyond the smallest magnitudes considered important, while the alternative places the effect inside a practically negligible interval. Rejecting that null supports equivalence within those bounds. Choosing bounds beforehand ties them to substantive judgment and prevents tailoring them to the observed estimate. A common implementation checks whether the appropriate confidence interval lies wholly within the prespecified lower and upper equivalence limits.
In a quality-control experiment, what does a non-significant difference between two manufacturing processes establish? Can it justify treating their defect rates as effectively the same?

Not automatically. A conventional difference test asks whether the data provide sufficient evidence against exact equality; failure to reject may simply reflect limited data. Treating processes as effectively the same requires a tolerance for the largest acceptable defect-rate difference and an analysis designed around it, such as an equivalence or noninferiority test. Precision, sampling plan, and possible process differences beyond the measured outcome also matter.
Suppose the estimated defect-rate difference is one percentage point, with a confidence interval from minus six to eight points. Why would a test of exact equality be uninformative here?

The interval is compatible with equality, but also with differences that may be operationally serious in either direction. A non-significant test of exact equality therefore cannot distinguish close similarity from inadequate precision. First define an acceptable margin, perhaps based on cost or safety. If the entire appropriately constructed interval fell inside that margin, the data could support practical equivalence; this interval plainly may not, depending on the chosen bounds.
I might be wrong, but I think failing to reject the null means the data provide sufficient evidence that the null hypothesis has been proven true? Would exact equality then be the conclusion?

No; non-rejection does not prove the null or supply affirmative evidence of exact equality. It says the chosen test did not find sufficient evidence against the null. With an interval from minus six to eight points, substantial differences remain compatible with the data, so imprecision is a central concern. If the goal is practical sameness, specify acceptable bounds and test whether the data are precise enough to exclude differences outside them.
If the acceptable margin were two percentage points, what sample-planning considerations would help an equivalence study produce an interpretable result rather than another wide interval?

Plan the sample size for adequate power to demonstrate equivalence within the two-point margin under plausible true differences and baseline defect rates. Account for unequal group sizes, clustering, missing observations, and repeated looks if relevant. Ensure measurement and sampling are comparable across processes. The target is enough precision for the confidence interval to fit inside the margin when the processes are genuinely close, while preserving the prespecified error rate.
